Appeal Court sentences Anon Nampa to prison for criticizing royal defamation law
The Appeal Court on 12 November sentenced human rights lawyer Anon Nampa to 4 years in prison on royal defamation and computer crimes charges for 3 Facebook posts which called for monarchy reform and criticized the use of the royal defamation law against critics of the monarchy.
Two of the posts, made on 1 January 2021, say that the royal defamation law should not be used to silence critics of the monarchy and that people should be able to talk about the monarchy when it comes to public matters even if they do not praise it. One of the posts also asks how losing faith in the monarchy could be an offense and if people are required to believe in the monarchy even if its members do not behave appropriately.
The third post, on 3 January 2021, criticized royalist groups for trying to silence dissidents when questions are raised about the monarchy. Anon wrote that royalists are refusing to see the problem when the problem is caused by the monarchy , such as lavish spending of the government’s money. He also asked if people would find it acceptable if the Prime Minister or other government official relocated to Germany and flew back and forth between Thailand and Germany with an entourage.
The complaint against Anon was filed by Nangnoi Assawakittikorn, a former member of the royalist group Thailand Help Centre for Cyberbullying Victims. Anon was later charged and indicted for royal defamation and violation of the Computer Crimes Act.
The Criminal Court on 17 January 2024 found Anon guilty and sentenced him to 4 years in prison. He subsequently filed an appeal.
Thai Lawyers for Human Rights (TLHR) reported that the Appeal Court upheld the January 2024 verdict of the Criminal Court. It ruled that although he referred to the monarchy in most of his posts, one post mentioned the King. after.summary:
Thailand must not return five Uyghurs to China, warn UN experts
The Government of Thailand must refuse to extradite five Uyghur men to the People’s Republic of China against their will, UN experts said today (13 November), warning that they were at real risk of serious and irreparable harm if returned.
Two individuals have even been transferred to immigration detention after completing their prison sentences and now await extradition.
“The mistreatment of the Uyghur minority in China is well-documented by UN human rights mechanisms, for example, in the OHCHR Assessment in August 2022, including arbitrary detention, enforced disappearance and torture based on ethnicity, culture, religion and national security,” the experts said.
“International law prohibits transferring a person to a country where there is a real risk of serious human rights violations, including arbitrary deprivation of life, torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, enforced disappearance, and persecution,” they said.
Thailand’s own Prevention and Suppression of Torture and Enforced Disappearance Act prohibits return of individuals where there are substantial grounds for believing they would be at risk of torture or enforced disappearance.
“Thailand’s obligation of non-refoulement applies to extradition as well as deportation,” the experts said. “It applies even if a person is accused of an offence.”
Measures to counter-terrorism and violent extremism measures in China have previously prompted concerns from UN experts. These have included mass arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances, torture and ill-treatment, mass surveillance, compulsory re-education, forced labour, restrictions on minority rights, and deaths in custody.
The five men now at risk are part of a larger group of over 350 Uyghurs who fled China and were detained near the Thai border in 2014. In 2015, Thailand deported 109 of them to China.

World leaders should increase pressure on Myanmar junta to end abuses, says Human Rights Watch
World leaders gathering in the Philippines on November 15-17, 2026, should more forcefully address the human rights and humanitarian crisis in Myanmar, Human Rights Watch said on 11 November. The East Asia Summit and Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and partner summits will include leaders of ASEAN nations and the United States, European Union, Japan, China, and India, among other countries.
In a November 5 letter to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. of the Philippines, the ASEAN chair and summit host, Human Rights Watch urged ASEAN not to recognize or endorse the sham elections earlier in 2026 that resulted in junta leader Min Aung Hlaing assuming Myanmar’s presidency. In recent months, several governments in ASEAN and the region have hosted Min Aung Hlaing, despite the junta’s rejection of ASEAN’s calls to address human rights and humanitarian issues. On November 11, the Philippine government confirmed that Min Aung Hlaing would not attend the summit. ASEAN partners should urge the bloc to continue blocking junta officials from representing Myanmar at ASEAN meetings, Human Rights Watch said.
“ASEAN could play an important role in bringing a stop to Myanmar military abuses,” said John Sifton, Asia advocacy director at Human Rights Watch. “Governments should be increasing pressure on the junta to end its attacks on civilians, lift restrictions on humanitarian aid, and begin credible dialogues about transitioning to civilian rule.”
As commander-in-chief of Myanmar’s military both before and after its 2021 military coup, Min Aung Hlaing has led numerous abusive military operations throughout the country, many including war crimes and crimes against humanity.

Former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra has applied for amnesty under the new Amnesty Act. His lawyer said he is seeking to clear his name to spend his old age out of politics.

The petition requested the Committee on Promoting a Peaceful Society to rule whether he is eligible for amnesty under the new amnesty law for political participation, formally called the Promotion of a Peaceful Society Act. Winyat said Thaksin is seeking to clear his name and that he does not wish to be involved in politics as he is getting older.
Thaksin is seeking amnesty for several corruption and misconduct charges filed against him for the 4-billion-Baht EXIM Bank loan, the two- and three-digit lottery project, the Shin Satellite concession modifications, and the 46-billion-Baht asset seizure. Amnesty would expunge his criminal records, and relieve him from all legal liabilities resulting from previous convictions. On 14 October, Winyat told The Nation that the petition covers cases he described as politically motivated and does not include the royal defamation charge for which Thaksin was acquitted in August 2025 and prosecutors have since appealed. He acknowledged that critics argue Thaksin’s convictions may fall within the law’s exclusions, particularly those covering corruption and misconduct, but stressed that filing a petition does not automatically entitle him to amnesty.

Appeal Court ruling puts Election Commission under renewed legal pressure
The Appeal Court has ruled that members of the public can directly file criminal lawsuits against Election Commission of Thailand (ECT) officials over alleged malfeasance in the 2024 Senate selection, bypassing the National Anti-Corruption Commission (NACC), which normally investigate allegations before cases can proceed to court.
The case stems from a lawsuit filed by a Senate candidate Phongsakorn Tangkittrakul against seven Election commissioners and ECT Secretary-General Sawaeng Boonme at the Chon Buri Provincial Court, accusing the eight of malfeasance for allowing the 2024 Senate selection to proceed without transparency and fairness.
The case was later referred to the Appeal Court President to determine whether it was within the Criminal Court for Corruption and Misconduct’s jurisdiction.
The Appeal Court ruling, issued on 6 November, stated that the Senate selection process misappropriated the sovereign power of Thai citizens, who were collectively victimised in the process, leaving them at liberty to bypass the NACC and directly file lawsuits against officials involved with the Criminal Court for Corruption and Misconduct.
The ruling overturned an earlier 5 May decision by the previous President which rejected Criminal Court for Corruption and Misconduct jurisdiction over the case.
According to Section 235 of the Constitution, a case which involves allegations against individuals holding positions in the independent institutions, including Constitutional Court and the ECT, must first be submitted to the NACC for further investigation. The NACC will then determine whether there are sufficient grounds to refer it on to the Criminal Court for Corruption and Misconduct.
The Organic Act on Criminal Procedure of Persons Holding Political Positions further stipulates that proceedings should be initiated by the Attorney-General or the NACC commissioners.

The Khon Kaen Provincial Court has dismissed a royal defamation charge filed against activist Songpol “Yajai” Sonthirak for flashing the three-finger salute at a graduation ceremony in December 2022.
Songpol was charged with royal defamation and violation of the Computer Crimes Act for flashing the three-finger “Hunger Games” salute, a well-known resistance symbol used by activists protesting the 2014 military coup and by students in the 2020 pro-democracy movement, after receiving his degree certificate from Princess Sirindhorn, King Vajiralongkorn’s younger sister, during Khon Kaen University’s graduation ceremony on 20 December 2022. He was also charged for an interview with The Isaan Record and another with a Khon Kaen University student activist group. He was indicted in November 2025.
Khon Kaen University reportedly paused its live broadcast of the graduation ceremony while Songpol and subsequent graduates from the Faculty of Law were receiving their certificates, and did not allow comments on the live broadcast after it resumed.
The complaint against him was filed by Kamon Kitkasiwat, leader of a royalist group in Khon Kaen, who was at the time an MP candidate for the royalist Thai Pakdee Party.
Thai Lawyers for Human Rights (TLHR) said today (10 November) that the Khon Kaen Provincial Court has dismissed the charge against Songpol. ECT challenges Supreme Court’s authority to examine Senate candidate qualifications
The Election Commission of Thailand (ECT) has sought a Constitutional Court ruling over the Supreme Court’s authority to examine the qualifications of Senate candidates, amid a controversy over the Senate selection fraud.
The ECT commissioners voted 5-2 to petition the Constitutional Court, asking it to rule whether the Supreme Court had the authority to examine the qualifications of five Senate candidates, two of whom are sitting senators, according to several news outlets.
Three petitions were filed with the Supreme Court by unsuccessful Senate candidates, known as reserve senators. They asked the Court to examine the qualifications of five Senate candidates who had passed the preliminary qualification examination conducted by the ECT. The ECT had judged that these candidates were eligible after an earlier petition filed over their qualifications.
The Supreme Court began reviewing the evidence in October 2025. The Court is expected to conclude the case by the end of this year.
However, the majority of the ECT commissioners claim that by accepting the petitions, the Supreme Court has infringed on the ECT’s authority to oversee the Senate selection process, particularly as these candidates had been officially cleared by the commission.
According to the ECT, the Supreme Court has no authority to initiate on its own the process to revisit the ECT’s final decision.
On 4 November, the ECT filed its petition with the Constitutional Court. The ECT argues that the law narrowly defines the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction, and gives it no authority to initiate investigations into electoral fraud, except in cases referred to the Supreme Court by the ECT itself.
